items.question: A motor insurer's claims portal generates a first-notification summary once the claimant submits a five-page web form. The generation takes 3.1 seconds and the claimant stares at a spinner for all of it. Analysis shows every input the prompt actually uses is captured by the end of page three, and claimants spend a median of 26 seconds on pages four and five. What is the highest-value change?

options.A: Increase the concurrency allocation for the summary endpoint so that submission-time bursts do not queue behind one another during peaks.
options.B: Reduce the summary's target length so that generation completes in under 2 seconds at the current tier.
options.C: Add a progress animation with staged status messages so the 3.1-second wait feels shorter to the claimant.
options.D: Dispatch the generation when page three is submitted, discarding the result if the claimant abandons or edits an input the prompt depends on.

items.question: A grant-making foundation screens applications with Claude. Measurement shows: 62% of input tokens are a static scoring rubric identical on every request; roughly 30% of requests within any hour are byte-identical resubmissions caused by a retry bug in the applicant portal; and responses average 1,400 tokens of which the consuming service reads only five structured fields, discarding the surrounding narrative. The board wants cost down without accepting any quality risk. Which THREE levers meet that constraint? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Place a cache breakpoint after the static rubric so the identical prefix is served from cache across requests.
options.B: Add a response store keyed on the normalised request so byte-identical resubmissions within the hour are served without a model call.
options.C: Move the workload to the cheapest tier, since screening is a bounded classification task with a fixed rubric.
options.D: Halve the rubric by removing its less frequently triggered criteria, cutting the largest single block of input tokens on every request the foundation makes.
options.E: Change the output contract so the model emits only the five consumed fields and no narrative.

items.question: Over a month, a Claude endpoint's p50 latency has been flat at 800ms while p99 has climbed from 3s to 9s. What does this pattern most strongly indicate, and where should investigation start?

options.A: The service is uniformly degrading and the median simply lags behind the tail; start by profiling the common request path against the last known-good trace captured before the trend began.
options.B: The percentile calculation is being distorted by low sample counts in the aggregation window; start by lengthening the window until the estimate stabilises across the month.
options.C: A minority sub-population of requests is behaving differently from the bulk; start by segmenting the tail requests and comparing their properties against the median population.
options.D: The provider's serving capacity has degraded for this account; start by comparing against published availability information.

items.question: An accountancy practice codes supplier invoices to ledger accounts. The original design used the strong tier at a cost index of 10 per invoice. The current design sends every invoice to the cheap tier (index 1), passes the result to a cheap verifier call (index 0.5), and escalates flagged items to the strong tier. In production the cheap tier is correct on 82% of invoices; the verifier flags about 95% of its errors plus roughly 4% of its correct answers, giving an escalation rate near 20% and a blended index of about 3.5. Roughly 0.9% of invoices are therefore coded wrongly and pass through unflagged. Which quantity, if it degrades over time, converts this design from a saving into a silent quality regression?

options.A: The escalation rate, because a rising rate erodes the blended cost advantage until the design is no cheaper than the original design.
options.B: The cheap tier's raw accuracy, because every point it loses is another point of mis-coded invoices entering the ledger.
options.C: The strong tier's cost index, because the blended figure depends on it and it is the largest term in the calculation.
options.D: The verifier's false-negative rate, because errors it passes are the only ones that reach the ledger and nothing downstream observes them.

items.question: A water utility's leak-report triage assistant escalates about 700 reports a week to human dispatchers when it cannot categorise them confidently. Dispatchers resolve and close each one in the work-management system with free-text notes. The team wants these escalations to drive the next round of improvements but currently has no way to say why the assistant failed on any of them. What is the next step?

options.A: Add a short mandatory structured reason code at escalation closure, chosen from a small fixed list derived from the failure patterns already known.
options.B: Have an engineer read a monthly sample of the free-text closure notes and write up the recurring themes for the improvement backlog and the next planning session.
options.C: Add a thumbs-up and thumbs-down control to the dispatcher console so escalated cases can be rated as the dispatcher works through them during the shift.
options.D: Send each escalated report back through the assistant with a prompt asking it to explain why it was unable to categorise the report and what further information would have helped.

items.question: Which of these production changes requires re-running the quality gate before it can ship?

options.A: Increasing the client's retry budget from two attempts to three.
options.B: Changing the pinned model version the feature calls.
options.C: Adding a second gateway region to the routing configuration.
options.D: Raising the p95 latency alert threshold from 2 seconds to 2.5 seconds.

items.question: A mid-size recruitment platform is launching a Claude-based candidate-shortlisting assistant next week. The operational dashboard already carries cost per completed shortlist. Which THREE further series must be present on day one? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Time to first token and end-to-end latency, maintained as separate percentile series.
options.B: A live tokens-per-second throughput gauge for the model calls, broken down by route and by model tier, refreshed continuously through the working day.
options.C: Task failure rate as experienced by the user, measured after retries are exhausted.
options.D: At least one quality proxy derived from an action recruiters already take, such as the rate at which a generated shortlist is edited before use.
options.E: A per-request trace link for every request, surfaced on the dashboard's front page.

items.question: A retail brokerage added a response cache to its market-commentary assistant, keyed on the normalised text of the user's question. Cache hit rate reached 44% and spend fell accordingly. Two weeks later compliance escalated: during a sharp intraday move, users asking about a specific holding received commentary generated ninety minutes earlier that described conditions that no longer existed. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Reduce the cache entry lifetime to five minutes, which bounds the staleness at an amount users are unlikely to notice.
options.B: Remove the response cache and rely on prompt caching of the stable instruction prefix, which produces savings without reusing generated content.
options.C: Include the identity and version of the underlying market data in the cache key, and invalidate entries when that data is refreshed.
options.D: Keep the cache but display the generation timestamp alongside each response so users can judge whether the commentary is still current.

items.question: Which statement best characterises the relationship between response length and latency for a Claude call, from an optimisation standpoint?

options.A: Generation time scales roughly with the number of output tokens produced, which usually makes output length the largest controllable term in the latency budget.
options.B: Input length dominates total latency, because the whole prompt must be processed before any output work can begin, and prompts are typically longer than responses.
options.C: Latency is set primarily by the model tier chosen for the call, with response length contributing only a minor and roughly constant term for any realistic response size.
options.D: Latency is largely independent of length in either direction, being dominated by network round trip, connection establishment and fixed gateway overhead on every call.

items.question: An HR software vendor serves 180 corporate tenants from one shared Claude-backed policy-answering service. Aggregate p95 is 1.4 seconds against a 2-second SLO and has been stable for months. One large tenant has raised a formal complaint that the feature is 'unusably slow', with screen recordings showing waits of six to eight seconds. The account is up for renewal in five weeks. What is the next step?

options.A: Provision a dedicated capacity pool for the complaining tenant so their requests cannot queue behind other tenants' traffic.
options.B: Move the tenant to a higher model tier for the renewal period, on the basis that a stronger tier will produce answers with less deliberation.
options.C: Raise the aggregate SLO target to 1 second so that the service is comfortably faster than the current complaint threshold for everyone.
options.D: Break the latency series down by tenant and correlate that tenant's requests against input token size, cache hit rate and retrieval result count.

items.question: A mining group's maintenance-planning agent consumes between 1 and 19 model calls per work order depending on how many equipment histories it needs to inspect. The platform team currently reports mean cost per API call, which has been flat for months, while the finance business partner insists the feature is over budget. Which TWO reporting changes resolve the disagreement? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Cap the agent at five model calls per work order so that the reported per-call figure becomes a reliable proxy for cost per completed task.
options.B: Aggregate spend by a task-level correlation identifier so every call belonging to one work order rolls up into a single figure.
options.C: Report cost per active user per month, which is the unit the finance partner budgets in.
options.D: Report the median and p95 of cost per completed work order rather than a single average.
options.E: Continue reporting mean cost per call but publish a confidence interval alongside it so the variability is visible.

items.question: A Claude feature is going live with no production history. What is the correct approach to setting its first alert thresholds?

options.A: Copy the thresholds from the most similar existing feature in the estate, since those were derived from real operating experience rather than guesswork or synthetic load.
options.B: Derive them from the load test, which characterised the system's behaviour under controlled and repeatable conditions.
options.C: Run in observation mode first, establish the real distribution of each signal, then set thresholds from those observed percentiles and the committed SLO.
options.D: Set them deliberately tight at launch so that any deviation is caught early, then relax them progressively as the team learns what normal traffic looks like.

items.question: A crop-science company's agronomy advisory assistant has fired its input-drift alert for the first time in eight months. Quality proxies have not yet moved. The model version is pinned, the prompt is unchanged, and a seasonal planting window opened nine days ago. Which TWO actions are appropriate before any change is made to the system? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Widen the retrieval result count so the assistant has more material to work with under the shifted question mix the alert has been reporting over the past nine days.
options.B: Establish whether the divergence reflects a real change in arriving requests or an artefact of comparing against a reference window that excludes this season.
options.C: Raise the drift threshold enough to stop repeat firing while the investigation runs, so the on-call rotation is not disturbed.
options.D: Score a fresh sample of current traffic against the labelled acceptance criteria to determine whether output quality has actually moved.
options.E: Roll back to the previously deployed model version to eliminate the model as a variable.

items.question: A children's learning platform runs an output-safety classifier over every generated tutoring response before it is shown. Generation takes 1.5 seconds and the classifier adds 900ms because it runs serially over the completed response, against a 2-second budget the product team will not relax. The classifier cannot be removed. What is the strongest latency change?

options.A: Skip the classifier for pupils whose accounts are marked as supervised by a teacher, halving the number of requests that incur the extra 900ms.
options.B: Stream the generated output into the classifier in segments so classification overlaps generation, releasing content only once each segment has cleared.
options.C: Move the classifier out of the request path and run it asynchronously after delivery, quarantining any response it later flags.
options.D: Replace the classifier with a larger, more capable model configured to return a single-token verdict, reducing the number of tokens it must generate.

items.question: How should error rate be defined for a production Claude feature so that the metric is operationally useful?

options.A: The proportion of upstream calls that returned a non-success status code, since that is the unambiguous machine-readable definition and the one every other service in the estate already uses for its own error budgets.
options.B: The proportion of calls that returned a non-success status code or were terminated by a client-side timeout.
options.C: The proportion of responses that a sampled human review judged to be substantively wrong.
options.D: The proportion of tasks that failed to yield a usable result for the consumer, counting transport failures, schema and validation failures, refusals where the task was legitimate, and downstream rejections.

items.question: An automotive dealer group's service-quote assistant had a p95 of 4.6 seconds. The team moved the parts-availability enrichment step out of the request path into a background job, and p95 immediately fell to 1.9 seconds. Three weeks later, service advisers report that quotes frequently arrive without parts availability and have to be re-requested, and the background job's failure rate turns out to be 7%. The latency dashboard still shows 1.9 seconds and the SLO is reported as met. What is the correct assessment?

options.A: The SLI no longer matches the adviser's journey; it must extend to the point a complete quote is available, and the 7% job failure rate must count against the error budget.
options.B: The change was sound and the remaining defect is reliability; adding retries and a dead-letter queue to the background job will resolve it without altering the latency measurement.
options.C: The enrichment should be returned to the request path, since deferring a step the user needs was the original error and the 4.6-second p95 was within tolerance.
options.D: The adviser reports are a training issue; advisers should be shown that the quote populates asynchronously and told to wait rather than re-requesting.

items.question: A hotel group's guest concierge assistant answers questions about a property using the property's policies, amenities, dining information and local guidance. These source documents change at most a few times a month. Every guest question currently triggers a synchronous call that reads the full source set and answers from it, and the interactive p95 is uncomfortably close to the 2.5-second budget. Which change most improves both cost and latency?

options.A: Raise the concurrency allocation for the concierge endpoint so requests do not queue during the evening check-in peak.
options.B: Instruct the model to answer more briefly, reducing generation time on every guest question at the property.
options.C: Precompute a condensed per-property briefing on the batch path when the source documents change, and answer guest questions from it.
options.D: Add a response cache keyed on the guest's question text so that repeated questions at the same property are served without a model call.

items.question: A university's student-services assistant runs on a fixed monthly departmental budget that finance will not increase mid-year. Usage is seasonal and unpredictable: clearing week and results week can quadruple volume without warning. Twice already the feature has hit its ceiling and been switched off entirely for the last four days of the month, which generated complaints and a formal escalation. What spend control should replace the hard cut-off?

options.A: Set a soft alert at 80% of budget so the team has early warning, and rely on manual intervention by the platform on-call, who can throttle or pause individual routes if consumption continues to climb toward the ceiling before month end.
options.B: Define burn-rate thresholds that progressively degrade service — deferring latency-tolerant work to the batch path, then routing low-stakes intents to a cheaper tier — while preserving the highest-value paths to the end of the period.
options.C: Introduce a per-student daily request quota sized so that the budget cannot be exhausted even at four times normal volume.
options.D: Move the entire workload to the batch path for the whole month, which brings the ceiling comfortably out of reach at any plausible volume.

items.question: Which production signal most directly indicates that a prompt change has made responses more verbose?

options.A: Mean and p95 output tokens per response rising, with request volume and task mix unchanged.
options.B: Total monthly spend rising against the previous month's figure.
options.C: End-to-end p95 latency rising while time to first token holds steady across the same reporting window.
options.D: The proportion of responses that reach the max_tokens ceiling increasing week on week across all routes.

items.question: A construction group is putting a Claude agent into production that tracks planning-permit applications across councils, calling several tools per task and looping until it can report a status. The team is adapting the dashboard it already uses for its single-call document-summarisation feature. Which THREE series must be added because the workload is agentic? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Steps per completed task, reported with its tail rather than only its mean.
options.B: Mean tokens per individual model call, trended daily and split by model tier and route.
options.C: Rate of tasks that terminate on the step or loop limit without producing a result.
options.D: Count of tools registered in the agent's configuration.
options.E: Tool-call error rate, broken down by individual tool.

items.question: A boutique wealth manager's client-briefing assistant handles about 300 requests a day. Its quality alert compares each day's adviser edit rate against a fixed baseline of 0.18 and fires when the day's figure exceeds 0.25. It fires roughly twice a week, and every investigation so far has found nothing — the following day returns to normal. The team is losing confidence in the metric. What should change?

options.A: Raise the alert boundary from 0.25 to 0.35 so that ordinary day-to-day variation at this volume no longer crosses it.
options.B: Alert on the absolute count of edited briefings per day rather than the rate, which removes the instability introduced by a small and variable daily denominator.
options.C: Evaluate the proxy over a window long enough to accumulate a stable sample and use bounds that widen as the sample shrinks, rather than a fixed daily boundary.
options.D: Stop alerting on the proxy and move it to the monthly operational review, where a whole month of traffic gives a reading reliable enough to act on with confidence.

items.question: A health insurer's benefits-explanation service has grown to be the third-largest line in the platform budget. The team has already trimmed the prompt, enabled prefix caching and moved every eligible job to the batch path. Fresh instrumentation reveals that 38% of all requests originate from one internal claims-workflow integration that re-asks the same member's question every five minutes while a case is open, each time with a fresh correlation identifier embedded in the request text. Nobody on the platform team owns that integration. What is the correct move?

options.A: Attribute spend by calling client, take the 38% figure and its cost to the integration's owning team, and make removing the redundant polling their change to fund and deliver.
options.B: Add a response cache that normalises out the correlation identifier so that the repeated questions are served from store without a further model call while the case remains open.
options.C: Apply a per-client rate limit to that integration so it cannot issue more than one request per case per hour.
options.D: Route that integration's traffic to the cheapest tier, since a repeated question about an already-open case does not need the strongest model to answer it acceptably.

items.question: A container shipping line's booking-amendment assistant has passed 100% of its regression suite on every release for four months. Over the same period, production escalations to human booking agents have risen steadily and the adviser edit rate has worsened. What should the team conclude?

options.A: The suite is performing correctly and the production deterioration must originate outside the assistant, most likely in an upstream system.
options.B: The release process is sound enough that the regression suite can be moved to a less frequent schedule, freeing capacity for feature work.
options.C: The pass criteria are too lenient and should be tightened so that near-misses within the existing cases start registering as failures.
options.D: The suite no longer represents the failures production is producing, and cases drawn from the current escalations need to be added to it.

items.question: Which TWO statements about prompt caching economics are accurate? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Caching reduces the number of output tokens the model generates for a given request.
options.B: Whether caching saves money depends on how often the identical prefix is re-read while an entry remains live.
options.C: Caching can be applied to whichever portion of the prompt contributes most to cost, regardless of where that portion sits.
options.D: Writing a cache entry costs more than sending the same tokens as ordinary input.
options.E: A cached segment is excluded from the model's context on subsequent requests, so both its cost and its latency contribution fall to zero.

items.question: A public broadcaster's archive-clearance workflow decides whether footage can be reused. On the current tier the workflow averages 4.1 model calls per completed clearance, because rejected drafts are re-run. A trial on the stronger tier, whose per-call cost index is 3.2 times higher, brings this to 1.3 calls per completed clearance and cuts the clearance officers' review time per case by 60%. The head of platform is preparing to reject the upgrade because per-call cost tripled. What is the correct recommendation?

options.A: Reject the upgrade: per-call cost is the line the platform team is accountable for, and tripling it cannot be justified by benefits accruing to another department.
options.B: Accept the upgrade: at 4.1 calls against 1.3 calls, API spend per completed clearance is essentially flat, and the 60% reduction in officer review time is the real saving.
options.C: Accept the upgrade on the grounds that fewer calls per clearance means substantially lower end-to-end latency for each case.
options.D: Reject the comparison as invalid: per-call cost indices from different tiers cannot be combined with call counts to produce a meaningful per-task figure.

items.question: A pet insurer runs claim triage on the cheap tier behind an inline quality gate that escalates failing responses to the stronger tier. The gate's rejection rate has jumped from 6% to 31% overnight. Escalation costs have risen accordingly, and the team's working assumption is that the cheap tier has degraded. What is the next step?

options.A: Escalate all triage traffic to the stronger tier until the cheap tier's behaviour has been characterised, accepting the additional cost for the duration of the investigation.
options.B: Sample the rejected responses and score them against the labelled acceptance criteria to establish how many were genuinely bad.
options.C: Check whether the gate itself changed — its prompt, its threshold, its model version or the schema it validates against — before investigating the cheap tier.
options.D: Compare the current input distribution against the reference window, since a shift in claim types would explain a sudden rise in cheap-tier failures.

items.question: A stadium operator's event-operations assistant has been through three cost-reduction efforts in two years. Each cut the prompt substantially; each time, within two quarters, the prompt had grown back past its previous size as engineers added clarifications, edge-case instructions and examples in response to individual defects. The architect wants the next reduction to hold. What mechanism achieves that?

options.A: Add a token-budget assertion to the pre-merge gate so a change that grows the prompt beyond its agreed budget fails the build unless the increase is explicitly approved with a measured justification.
options.B: Schedule a prompt-cleanup sprint each quarter to remove accumulated additions before they compound.
options.C: Record the token budget in the feature's runbook, publish it to the team, and cover prompt size as a standing item in the monthly operational review alongside cost per completed task.
options.D: Require that any engineer adding to the prompt removes an equivalent number of tokens elsewhere in the same change, keeping the budget flat by construction and enforced at code review by the owning team.

items.question: An ambulance service's clinical-triage adjunct summarises caller information for dispatchers. The team reports p95 latency at 1.2 seconds against a 2-second commitment and the SLO shows green every week. Dispatchers, however, consistently describe waits of four to six seconds during busy periods. The client wrapper retries on a 2-second timeout with up to two additional attempts, and each attempt is recorded as its own measurement in the latency series. What is wrong?

options.A: The p95 is being computed over too short an aggregation window, so busy-period behaviour is averaged away against quiet periods.
options.B: The 2-second client timeout is set too close to the commitment, so requests that would have completed acceptably are being cut short and retried unnecessarily during busy periods, inflating both load and cost.
options.C: Retries should be excluded from the latency series entirely, since a retried attempt is a failure rather than a latency observation.
options.D: The series measures individual attempts rather than the dispatcher's wait; a request that times out twice and succeeds on the third contributes three fast-looking observations while the dispatcher waited for all of them.

items.question: A drift detector on a production Claude feature has not fired once in fourteen months. What should the team do before concluding that the input distribution has been stable?

options.A: Lower the divergence threshold until the detector begins producing occasional firings, then settle it just above that point.
options.B: Verify that the detector can fire, by replaying traffic with a known injected shift and confirming it is detected end to end.
options.C: Cross-check the conclusion against the quality proxy, which would have degraded if meaningful drift had occurred.
options.D: Extend the reference window so the comparison spans a longer and therefore more reliable baseline period.

items.question: Which THREE facts must be established before an existing synchronous production workload is moved to the asynchronous batch path? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: That no consumer — human or downstream service — is blocked waiting on any individual result.
options.B: That the batch path yields better output quality, since generation on that path is not constrained by an interactive time budget or by client timeouts.
options.C: That the job's completion deadline has slack beyond the turnaround the team has actually measured for its own batch jobs.
options.D: That the prompts used are shorter than those sent on the synchronous path.
options.E: That a fallback exists for results still outstanding when the deadline approaches, with a checkpoint early enough for it to complete.

items.question: A pharmacy chain's prescription-interaction check runs inside the dispensing workflow under a 1.8-second p95 commitment negotiated with the clinical governance committee; current p95 is 1.55 seconds. A proposed change — consolidating three short model calls into one longer reasoning call — would cut spend on the workload by 30% but adds an estimated 400ms to p95. Roughly 40% of the workload is overnight repeat-dispensing checks with no pharmacist waiting. How should the architect proceed?

options.A: Ship the change and open a renegotiation with the clinical governance committee to move the commitment to 2 seconds, supported by the cost saving.
options.B: Reject the change: a 400ms addition against 250ms of headroom breaches a clinical commitment, and no cost saving justifies that.
options.C: Apply the change only to the overnight repeat-dispensing traffic, where the latency commitment does not bind, and keep the interactive path on the existing design.
options.D: Ship the change to all traffic and recover the 400ms by removing the interaction-history retrieval step, which is the next largest contributor to the trace.

items.question: Which TWO properties must every alert on a production Claude feature have to be worth configuring? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A threshold set at the 99th percentile of the values observed during the baselining period.
options.B: A documented action the recipient can take, recorded in the runbook against that alert.
options.C: Automatic suppression after three firings within an hour, to protect the recipient from repeated notification.
options.D: A defined relationship to a user-visible SLO or to a budget the team has committed to.
options.E: An escalation path that notifies the feature's product owner if the alert is not acknowledged within a set period.

items.question: A recruitment-marketing agency shipped a single prompt change on Monday that did three things at once: added six worked examples, added a step-by-step reasoning instruction, and expanded the retrieved context from three documents to eight. Since then, cost per completed task is up 96% and the reviewer edit rate has improved from 0.31 to 0.22. The budget holder will fund the increase only if it is necessary. What is the next step?

options.A: Test the three modifications separately against the same case set to establish which of them produced the quality gain and at what individual cost.
options.B: Revert the change and reintroduce it in the next cycle, once a full cost-benefit analysis has been prepared and signed off by the budget holder and the delivery lead.
options.C: Keep the change and present the edit-rate improvement as the justification, since a nine-point movement on the quality proxy is a strong result by any standard.
options.D: Keep the change and offset the cost by moving the workload to the cheapest tier that still holds the new edit rate at its improved level over a full week.

items.question: A fashion retailer scores every one of its 400,000 daily product-description generations with a second Claude call that rates the description against a rubric, producing a continuous quality proxy. Finance has pointed out that the scoring calls now cost more than the generation calls, because the scoring prompt includes the full rubric while the generation prompt does not. What should the team do?

options.A: Keep scoring every generation but move the scoring calls to the asynchronous batch path, since nothing downstream waits on an individual score and the trend is only consumed once a day.
options.B: Stop the automated scoring and rely on the merchandising team's existing rejection rate as the quality proxy instead.
options.C: Keep full coverage and move the scorer to the cheapest tier, holding the rubric and the rest of the scoring prompt identical to what runs today so the series is unaffected.
options.D: Score a stratified sample — all flagged or unusual generations plus a few per cent of ordinary ones — since a trend needs enough observations to be stable, not complete coverage.

items.question: A disaster-relief NGO runs a Claude system that triages inbound field reports into severity bands and routes them to response teams. A major flooding event has pushed volume to twenty times normal and it will stay there for days. The monthly budget is fixed and donor-restricted with no possibility of increase. Severe reports need routing within seconds; low-severity reports can wait. Misclassifying a severe report as low is the failure that costs lives; the reverse merely wastes responder time. The system currently sends every report to the strong tier and, at twenty times volume, will exhaust the budget in four days. What should the architect do?

options.A: Move all triage to the cheapest tier for the duration of the event, accepting a uniformly higher error rate across every severity band in exchange for staying inside the fixed budget for the whole of the response operation rather than only its first four days.
options.B: Run every report through the cheap tier first with an inline gate biased towards escalation, send anything the gate flags as possibly severe to the strong tier, and monitor the escalation rate and a sampled audit of unescalated reports throughout.
options.C: Keep the strong tier for all reports and queue the overflow, processing in arrival order so that no report is triaged with a weaker model.
options.D: Keep the strong tier and halve the prompt by removing the severity-band definitions and worked examples, which are the largest input blocks.

items.question: A mobile network operator spent six weeks tuning its tier-1 support assistant against an LLM-judge rubric scoring accuracy, completeness and tone on a five-point scale. The mean judge score rose from 3.9 to 4.4, and every weekly iteration was accepted on that basis. Over the same six weeks CSAT on assisted chats fell four points and the fastest-growing complaint tag became 'didn't get to the point'. The prompt has been rolled back and CSAT has recovered. Before the team attempts the next quality push, what must change?

options.A: Increase the number of cases scored per iteration so that a movement of half a point in the mean is comfortably outside the suite's noise band before anyone treats it as a gain.
options.B: Add an adversarial and jailbreak suite to the acceptance criteria, so that a tuning run chasing completeness cannot quietly trade away safety behaviour at the same time.
options.C: Establish that the rubric's dimensions track the outcome the operator is judged on, by hand-labelling a sample of chats for resolution and re-weighting or removing dimensions that do not move with it.
options.D: Replace model-graded scoring with exact-match comparison against reference answers written by senior agents, so iteration is measured against a fixed target rather than another model's preference.

items.question: A motor insurer summarises claim files for adjusters. To reduce spend the team moved the summariser to a cheaper model tier and trimmed the prompt. Monthly model spend fell by about a third, and the 200-item golden set, graded by similarity to reference summaries, was unchanged within its interval. Eleven weeks later the claims audit team reports that the rate at which adjuster decisions are overturned on internal appeal has risen by half; sampled appeals show the same pattern, in which a prior-damage note or a policy endorsement present in the file is absent from the summary. Which finding best explains why the validation passed a change that harmed the downstream decision?

options.A: Similarity to a reference summary barely moves when one decision-relevant sentence is dropped from a long passage, so the metric could not register the failure adjusters experience.
options.B: The 200-item golden set was too small to resolve a change of this magnitude, so the flat result was an underpowered null being read as evidence of no harm.
options.C: The change bundled a tier downgrade with a prompt trim, so the flat result could not be attributed to either component and should never have been accepted.
options.D: Similarity scoring should have been replaced by a model judge, which detects quality differences between two fluent summaries that overlap-based metrics are known to miss.

items.question: A freight brokerage monitors the embedding distribution of inbound carrier emails against a fixed reference window. A population-stability alert fires on Monday and stays elevated all week. The model version is pinned and unchanged, the prompt registry shows no deploy in three weeks, and both sampled quality scores and the field-extraction error rate are flat. Operations confirms that a large new customer began sending load tenders on a different template on Friday evening. What is the correct response?

options.A: Rebuild the drift detector's reference distribution from the current week's traffic, so the monitor returns to baseline and stops reporting a condition that both the sampled quality scores and the extraction error rate currently contradict.
options.B: Treat the alert as a change in the input population rather than in system behaviour: extend the eval set and per-segment quality reporting to cover the new template, and keep the alert open as a coverage signal until they do.
options.C: Roll back to the previous prompt version, because a drift alert that persists for a week with no other explanation points to the most recent change to the request path.
options.D: Suppress the input-drift monitor for this pipeline, since sampled quality scoring measures the outcome directly and a leading indicator that disagrees with it adds only noise.

items.question: An industrial equipment manufacturer generates field-service reports from technician notes plus retrieved excerpts of service manuals. A cost programme removed the few-shot examples and compressed the retrieved excerpts; token spend per report fell by 40% and the aggregate eval score was unchanged. Two months later the warranty team finds that reports increasingly cite superseded part numbers, which invalidates the warranty claims built from them. (Choose TWO.) Which two measurements, in place at the time of the change, would have exposed the regression before the warranty team found it?

options.A: A per-report token count and cost dashboard with an alert when either moves outside its expected band, giving early visibility of the change's effect.
options.B: A field-level check of every cited part number against the parts master, scored as a pass rate on the same report set before and after the change.
options.C: A grounding check confirming that each part number cited in the report appears in the excerpt the report was generated from, run on the compressed and uncompressed pipelines over identical inputs.
options.D: A latency breakdown by pipeline stage, to confirm that compression moved time out of generation without pushing it into the retrieval and ranking stages, and that the p95 for report production stayed inside the field team's budget.
options.E: An increase in the judge model's sampling temperature, so that near-identical reports receive a wider spread of scores and small differences become visible.

items.question: At 09:10 a rail operator's crew-rostering assistant begins producing rosters that violate a minimum-rest rule. The on-call engineer has already flipped the feature flag routing all requests to the deterministic legacy roster builder, so no further bad rosters reach dispatchers. The assistant is a multi-step agent whose full trajectories go to a trace store with seven-day retention. The runtime prompt, tool definitions and model parameters are served from a config service that keeps only the current revision. The engineer's next action is to roll the config service back to yesterday's revision. What must happen before that rollback?

options.A: Raise the trace store's retention from seven days to ninety, so that no trajectory relevant to the investigation ages out while the postmortem is being written.
options.B: Export the current revision in full — prompt text, tool definitions, model id and parameters — together with the trajectory ids for the affected window, so the failing configuration can be reconstructed after it is overwritten.
options.C: Run the full regression suite against the live configuration to confirm that it reproduces the rest-rule violation, so that the fault is established and documented against the running system before any component of it is changed.
options.D: Notify the safety regulator, because a rest-rule breach is a reportable event and the notification must be filed before remediation alters the system's state.

items.question: A team uses a single LLM-judge score both as the target it iterates prompts against and as the criterion its release gate enforces. What is the principal risk?

options.A: Judge scores are not comparable across grader model versions, so the gate's threshold has to be re-derived from scratch after every grader upgrade or the trend breaks.
options.B: Model-graded scores carry more run-to-run variance than deterministic checks, so a gate defined on them will produce intermittent false failures that erode trust in the pipeline.
options.C: Iteration selects for whatever the judge happens to reward, so the score keeps climbing while the quality it stands for does not, and the gate loses the ability to refuse the change.
options.D: Position bias inflates the score of whichever candidate the judge sees second, so improvements measured in a pairwise setup will not survive a switch to absolute scoring.

items.question: A benefits agency generates plain-language explanations of entitlement decisions. To cut cost the team lowered the maximum output token cap. Spend fell, and the 300-case eval suite, whose reference answers average about 180 words, showed no change on any metric. Two weeks later caseworkers report that explanations for households with several concurrent claims 'stop in the middle of a sentence'. Which control would have caught this before release, and why?

options.A: A canary at 5% of traffic gated on the aggregate judge score, because the affected explanations would have pulled the cohort's mean below the gate's threshold during the ramp.
options.B: A latency guardrail on the generation stage, because capping output tokens changes how long generation runs and the change should have surfaced as a shift in the latency profile.
options.C: A judge rubric criterion for fluency, because an explanation cut off mid-sentence reads as disfluent and would score below the threshold on that dimension.
options.D: Monitoring of the output-length distribution and the reason each generation stopped, because the eval corpus's short answers never approach the new cap that long multi-claim cases exceed.

items.question: A food-delivery marketplace runs an order-issue resolver. At 18:40 the rolling quality score, a model-graded audit of sampled resolutions, drops from 0.88 to 0.71 and stays down through the dinner peak, recovering at 21:30. No deploy occurred. The gateway is configured to fall back to a smaller model when requests to the primary are throttled, throttling counts were elevated across the same window, and every request logs the model id that actually served it. Which analysis will most directly confirm or eliminate the fallback path as the cause?

options.A: Split the audit sample by the model id that served each request and compare the score within each path across the window and against the preceding days.
options.B: Replay the affected requests against the primary model now that throttling has cleared, and compare the new responses with what was originally served.
options.C: Re-score the same audit sample with a second judge configuration, to rule out grader instability during the window before pursuing a serving explanation.
options.D: Compare the dinner-peak score against the same peak on each of the previous seven days, to establish whether a drop at this hour is a recurring seasonal pattern.

items.question: A broadcaster's archive-tagging service has twice been unable to attribute a quality change after the fact, because the request log records only the input, the output and a timestamp. Storage review will approve exactly three additional per-request fields. (Choose THREE.) Which three fields carry attribution value for a future quality investigation?

options.A: The model id and version string as reported by the API for that specific request.
options.B: A version tag for the resolved prompt template together with a hash of the variable values injected into it.
options.C: The identifier of the retrieval index snapshot the request read from.
options.D: The character length of the response body, so that shifts in verbosity can be tracked over time without parsing stored outputs.
options.E: The judge score of the nearest matching case in the golden set, attached at request time as a quality expectation for that input.

items.question: An e-commerce retailer ships small prompt refinements to its product-description generator most weeks. Each release is gated on a comparison against the immediately preceding release over a 500-item suite, requiring no regression worse than one point; the suite is resampled from production traffic each quarter and graders are blind to which release produced which output. Fourteen consecutive releases have passed. A merchandising manager pulls descriptions from a year ago and from today, and a blind hand-grading of 100 pairs shows a large preference for the year-old set. Which flaw in the gate allowed this?

options.A: Each release was compared only against its immediate predecessor, so a loss just inside tolerance could repeat week after week and accumulate without any single comparison ever failing.
options.B: The gate used a fixed threshold rather than a confidence interval, so releases whose measured difference fell inside the suite's noise band were recorded as passes rather than as indeterminate results.
options.C: Automated grading and human preference measure different constructs, so agreement between the gate and the manager's hand-grading was never a reasonable expectation in the first place.
options.D: Fourteen releases against the same style of suite fitted the prompts to the suite's cases, so the measured scores stopped generalising to production descriptions some releases ago.

items.question: A retail bank's chat assistant handles 100,000 conversations a month. Before the change, model spend was $0.12 per conversation and 60% of conversations were resolved without a human agent; each escalation costs the contact centre $6.00. The team moved to a cheaper model tier: model spend fell to $0.05 per conversation and the resolved-without-agent rate fell to 52%. The offline eval suite showed a one-point drop, inside the gate's tolerance, so the change shipped. (Choose TWO.) Which two statements follow from these figures?

options.A: Monthly model spend falls by $7,000 while the total monthly cost of the channel rises by $41,000.
options.B: Total channel cost falls by $7,000 a month, since escalation handling is funded from the contact centre's budget rather than the platform's.
options.C: The gate's tolerance is correctly calibrated for this system, because a one-point drop on the eval suite corresponds to roughly a one-point drop in the resolution rate.
options.D: The change adds 8,000 escalations a month, costing $48,000, which exceeds the entire model spend under either configuration.
options.E: Break-even would require the cheaper tier to hold the resolution rate within about three points of the original, which the observed eight-point fall only narrowly misses.

items.question: An energy retailer audits 500 sampled customer emails a day with an LLM judge and tracks a rolling quality score. Overnight the score falls from 0.90 to 0.84 and stays there. The drop appears in every customer segment, every channel and every prompt variant at close to the same magnitude. No application deploy or corpus refresh occurred, the serving-path log shows the pinned primary model served every request in the window, and inbound volume is normal. The judging service resolves its grader from a floating alias. What is the first hypothesis to test, and how?

options.A: A change in the input population: check whether an upstream system began routing a different mix of email types into the pipeline overnight, which would move the blended score without any component of the system behaving differently.
options.B: A genuine broad regression: begin rolling back the most recent application release and watch whether the score recovers over the following audit windows.
options.C: A change in the measurement itself: re-score an archived sample of pre-drop outputs through today's judging service and compare with the scores those same outputs originally received.
options.D: A silent capacity-driven fallback: check whether some share of requests was quietly served by a different model tier during the overnight window.

items.question: A budgeting app shows a generated spending insight with thumbs-up and thumbs-down controls, and the team tracks thumbs-down rate as its main quality proxy. In the week of a mobile release the rate doubles. The model, the prompt and the data pipeline are unchanged, and the weekly hand-graded audit of 100 insights is flat. The mobile release moved the feedback control out of a collapsed menu and onto the insight card itself. (Choose TWO.) Which two conclusions are supported by this evidence?

options.A: The unchanged audit proves that no user-visible quality change occurred, since 100 hand-graded items is ample to detect an effect large enough to double a feedback rate.
options.B: The proxy is not comparable across the release boundary, because moving the control changes which users see it and how likely they are to use it.
options.C: Explicit feedback should be retired in favour of a model-graded score computed on every response, because volunteered signals are too unreliable to be worth collecting.
options.D: The count of thumbs-down events can rise purely through greater exposure of the control, with no change in the underlying distribution of user opinion.
options.E: Because the model did not change, the increase must originate in another part of the mobile release, such as a rendering defect in how insights are displayed.

items.question: A hospital group drafts discharge summaries with Claude; a clinician reviews, edits and signs each one before it goes to the receiving practice. The quality the medical director cares about — whether a draft ever leaves the receiving clinician with a wrong understanding of the patient — is not recorded anywhere and cannot be observed at scale. The team must choose proxies it can compute over all drafts. (Choose TWO.) Which two proxies carry evidence about that construct?

options.A: The median elapsed time between draft generation and clinician signature, tracked per department and per grade of signing clinician.
options.B: The mean judge score for readability and structure of the draft, computed on every summary against a fixed rubric maintained by the clinical documentation team and reported to the medical director each month alongside volume.
options.C: A recurring audit that checks each draft against the source record for a fixed list of must-carry facts, reported as recall over that list.
options.D: The proportion of drafts signed with no edit at all, read as the clinician's agreement with the draft exactly as it was generated.
options.E: The rate at which the signing clinician's edits change clinical content — medication, dose, diagnosis, follow-up — rather than wording, obtained by classifying the diff between draft and signed version.

items.question: Under covariate shift the distribution of inputs changes; under concept drift the correct output for an unchanged input changes. What does each imply for an existing labelled golden set?

options.A: Covariate shift invalidates the labels, because they were assigned under a different input distribution; concept drift changes only the mix, so stratified reweighting of the existing set is sufficient.
options.B: Covariate shift leaves existing labels valid but makes the set unrepresentative, so resample inputs; concept drift invalidates the labels themselves, so the affected items must be re-adjudicated.
options.C: Both require relabelling from scratch, because in either case the mapping the set encodes no longer matches the mapping production is being asked to reproduce.
options.D: Neither affects the golden set, whose purpose is to be a fixed baseline; both are handled by adding a separate rolling sample drawn from current production traffic.

items.question: An airline placed a semantic cache in front of its disruption-rebooking assistant: a query whose embedding is close enough to a stored one is answered from the stored response. The hit rate reached 41% and model spend fell accordingly. Quality is measured by an offline suite of anonymised, generic queries, which is unchanged. Customer relations forwarded three cases where a passenger was told about a rebooking option belonging to a different itinerary; as an immediate mitigation the cache has already been disabled for itinerary-specific queries. What should the team do next?

options.A: Raise the similarity threshold across the board until the hit rate falls to a level the team is comfortable with, trading part of the saving for a wider margin of safety.
options.B: Add the three reported cases to the offline suite as regression items and re-run it, so the suite fails if the same confusion is reintroduced later.
options.C: Sample live cache hits from the remaining traffic, compute the uncached answer for each on a shadow path, and measure how often the served answer differs materially from it.
options.D: Replace the embedding model with a higher-dimensional one so that queries differing only in itinerary details are less likely to fall within the match radius.

items.question: A legal services firm's contract-review agent shows cost per reviewed contract up 3.1 times over five weeks. Contract volume, model tier and commercial terms are unchanged, and both final-answer accuracy and p95 latency are flat. The finance partner wants the mechanism identified before the next billing cycle, and the plausible mechanisms are longer inputs per step, more steps per contract, and reduced reuse of the cached prompt prefix. Which analysis distinguishes them?

options.A: Split total spend into model spend, retrieval infrastructure and orchestration compute, identify which line item grew over the five weeks, and reconcile the result against the invoice the finance partner will receive.
options.B: Split cost per contract into steps per contract, input tokens per step separated into cache-read and freshly processed, and output tokens per step, then compare each factor with its value five weeks ago.
options.C: Split cost by client segment and contract type, to find which cohort is pulling the average upwards.
options.D: Split cost by hour of day, to see whether the increase coincides with the overnight bulk-review window rather than interactive use.

items.question: An education platform's grading assistant trips its quality alert twenty minutes after the nightly reindex of the rubric corpus completed. The release log shows no model, prompt or code change in the past four days. What is the first step?

options.A: Raise the alert threshold, since a single alert immediately following a routine scheduled job is most likely noise from the sampling window.
options.B: Roll the model back to the previously pinned version and watch whether the alert clears over the next few sampling windows.
options.C: Open a full postmortem and schedule an expansion of the eval set for the rubric categories that scored lowest in the alerting window.
options.D: Check what the reindex changed, by replaying a set of requests against the old and new index and comparing the retrieved rubric passages.

items.question: A workforce-management SaaS ships model downgrades behind a quality gate: the candidate must score within half a point of the incumbent on a frozen 400-case suite. The suite was frozen fourteen months ago. Since then the product onboarded a large public-sector customer whose shift-pattern vocabulary appears nowhere in the suite and which now accounts for 22% of traffic. A downgrade passed the gate last month, and public-sector tickets about misread shift patterns have risen sharply since. (Choose TWO.) Which two changes to the gate address the cause?

options.A: Unfreeze the suite and resample it from current production traffic before every gate run, so the gate always reflects the traffic of the week in which it runs.
options.B: Tighten the pass tolerance from half a point to a quarter of a point, so that smaller aggregate regressions are enough to block a downgrade.
options.C: Add a coverage check that compares the suite's case mix against current production traffic and blocks the gate when a segment above a defined share of traffic is unrepresented.
options.D: Replace the pre-release gate with a live A/B test on 5% of traffic and make that test the sole criterion for accepting a downgrade.
options.E: Require the gate to evaluate its threshold per segment for every segment above a defined share of traffic, rather than only on the aggregate score.

items.question: A payments provider's dispute-response drafter produced a response citing a chargeback reason code that does not exist, and the response reached a merchant before a reviewer caught it. Root cause analysis found that for one rare combination of card network and reason category, retrieval returned no document above the relevance floor and the model filled the gap from its own priors. (Choose TWO.) Which two actions convert this incident into durable protection?

options.A: Add the exact failing input, together with constructed near-neighbours that share the empty-retrieval property, as blocking cases in the regression suite.
options.B: Add a sentence to the system prompt instructing the model never to invent reason codes, and close the incident on that basis.
options.C: Raise the retrieval top-k for this drafter so that rare network and category combinations return candidate documents instead of an empty set.
options.D: Emit a production signal whenever a response is generated with no retrieved document above the relevance floor, and alert when its rate exceeds a defined level.
options.E: Re-run the adversarial jailbreak suite against the drafter to confirm that no related safety regression was introduced in the same period.

items.question: A team wants to gate releases on a proxy metric that stands in for an outcome it cannot measure at release time. What must be established before the proxy can carry that weight?

options.A: That the proxy can be computed on every production request rather than on a sample, so that the gate never has to decide on partial data.
options.B: That the proxy moves with the outcome on a labelled sample, and that the relationship is re-checked whenever the system or the traffic changes materially.
options.C: That the proxy has lower run-to-run variance than the outcome it replaces, so that pass and fail decisions are stable across repeated runs.
options.D: That the proxy is produced by a model from a different family than the one under test, so that self-preference cannot inflate the reported score.

items.question: A national tax authority's guidance assistant reports a weekly quality score: the mean model-graded score across all audited responses. This week the overall score fell from 0.86 to 0.82. The segment dashboard shows that each of the four question categories — registration, filing, payments and appeals — scored higher this week than last. A penalty-notice mailing went out on Monday, and appeals questions, the category with the lowest absolute scores, rose from 8% to 26% of volume. What should the team report, and what follow-up does the evidence justify?

options.A: Report the four-point fall as a regression and open an incident on the assistant, because the aggregate is the figure the service has committed to in its published quality target and the segment view is an internal diagnostic.
options.B: Report the per-category figures and retire the aggregate, because a mean taken over a population whose composition moves is not an interpretable quantity.
options.C: Report both figures without adjustment and wait a further week, because one week's movement cannot be separated from ordinary variation at this sample size.
options.D: Report a mix-adjusted score holding last week's category weights fixed, note that quality rose within every category, and point follow-up at appeals capacity and content rather than at a regression.

items.question: What does 'cost per successfully completed task' capture that 'cost per API call' does not?

options.A: It prices retries, multi-step trajectories and the calls that produce no usable result, so a change that makes calls cheaper while success becomes rarer registers as a cost increase.
options.B: It expresses spend in the unit that finance already works in, which is what allows an AI budget to be set against other operating line items and defended in an annual planning cycle without further conversion.
options.C: It removes the effect of prompt caching from the reported figure, giving a baseline that is stable across warm and cold cache states.
options.D: It separates model spend from the surrounding infrastructure spend, which is a precondition for any meaningful comparison between two model tiers.

items.question: A travel platform's itinerary assistant reuses a large static system prompt across requests and depends on prefix caching for its unit economics. After a release, monthly spend rises sharply while latency, error rate and every quality metric stay flat. The release added a line near the top of the system prompt rendering the current date and time to the second. The offline eval harness builds each case in a fresh process and never reuses a prefix between cases, so the harness's own run cost is unaffected by prefix stability. Which control belongs in the pre-merge pipeline to prevent this class of defect?

options.A: A cost regression test that runs the eval suite on every pull request and fails the build when the run's total spend exceeds the previous run's by more than a set percentage, with the threshold reviewed each quarter.
options.B: A review checklist item requiring an engineer to confirm that any newly added system-prompt content is static before the change can be approved.
options.C: An assertion that the cacheable prefix is byte-identical across two requests built from different inputs, failing the build when a change makes the prefix vary per request.
options.D: A production alert on cost per request, with a threshold derived from the trailing week's mean and standard deviation for that endpoint.

items.question: At 11:05 a health insurer's prior-authorisation summariser trips its quality alert; the audited score for the last hour is well below the band. The full regression suite is 2,000 cases and takes about six hours. A pre-defined 120-case triage subset, stratified over request types, runs in under ten minutes. The last configuration change was nine days ago. The declared fallback is manual review by nurses, which the utilisation-review team can absorb for a few hours but not for a day. What is the next step?

options.A: Divert all traffic to manual review immediately and start the six-hour full suite, accepting the nursing workload for the remainder of the day as the price of removing any possibility of a bad summary reaching a clinician.
options.B: Run the 120-case triage subset against the live configuration, establishing within minutes whether the regression reproduces away from live traffic, before deciding whether to divert.
options.C: Roll back to the configuration that preceded the most recent change and watch whether the audited score recovers over the next hour.
options.D: Have the clinical team hand-grade fifty live responses to confirm the alert is real before committing to any automated suite run.
